messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Film Director
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark)., Meaning Seeking: I think about why the event has happened to me, Distraction: I distract myself with something else
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Inadequacy: I am inadequate, Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Matthias is a 52-year-old film director who came to treatment months after a life-threatening accident on location that still feels to him less like something that happened in the past than something waiting just off camera. During a night shoot in a remote industrial area, a lighting rig failed and crashed as a vehicle was being repositioned. In the confusion that followed, power dropped out across part of the set, leaving stretches of sudden darkness broken by harsh work lights, shouted instructions, and the metallic blast of equipment hitting concrete. Matthias was knocked down and briefly trapped amid cables and debris, convinced for several seconds that another collapse was coming and that he might die before anyone reached him. What remains with him now is not a coherent story but a sequence of sharp images: the angled glare of a work lamp, sparks, the black gap beyond the set, a twisted stand descending into view. He says the memory is extraordinarily clear and detailed, yet when he tries to describe it aloud he loses his words and becomes frustrated, as if the event exists in pictures his mind can replay but not translate.

That quality of memory has worn on his sense of himself. Because the accident returns in these vivid, mostly visual fragments that he cannot fully put into language, Matthias has come to believe there is something fundamentally inadequate about him. He compares his current state to the composed, decisive director he had always known himself to be and thinks, with shame, that his reactions prove he is a lousy coper. At times he says he barely recognizes the man he has become: someone derailed by a moment on his own set, unable even to give a straightforward account of it.

Those conclusions have shaped how he lives day to day. Convinced that his ongoing reactions mean weakness rather than injury, he works hard to manage them privately. He distracts himself relentlessly, burying himself in editing notes, streaming rough cuts late into the night, or scrolling through production schedules whenever his mind drifts toward the accident. He also finds himself circling the same unanswerable question—why this happened to him, why on a set he was responsible for, why he was the one who cannot seem to move on. Most concretely, he avoids circumstances that remind him of that night, especially darkness. He has started insisting on overlit rooms at home and on set, delegating night exterior shoots when he can, lingering in his trailer until others have checked locations first. The more he sees these maneuvers as necessary, the more they seem to confirm his view that he is no longer capable in the way he once was.

At work, the sensory world of filmmaking has become a minefield. Unexpected bangs from dropped equipment, a slammed stage door, or a sound cue played too loudly can make him jolt violently. He scans constantly for what might go wrong, listening for changes in the room and tracking crew movement with a vigilance he did not have before. Those reactions are tied not only to the set environment but to the way the accident lives in his mind: a sudden metallic crash or the hum-and-cut of power can call up the image of the rig falling so quickly that his body responds before he has fully registered where he is. Once that happens, he becomes even more watchful, certain that if he lets his guard down he will be caught off balance again.

That sense of threat feeds directly into further avoidance. If a sound check is chaotic or a generator backfires, Matthias may abruptly step away under the pretense of taking a call, then remain in brighter, quieter areas for the rest of the shift. He tells himself he is being practical, but his world has narrowed. Crew members have noticed he is less available during complicated setups, and his partner has noticed that he keeps lamps on throughout the apartment and changes the subject when the accident comes up. His attempts to distract himself and stay away from reminders have not softened the memory. If anything, the images intrude more forcefully in the spaces he is trying to outrun, and because he never stays with them long enough to make them into a fuller narrative, they remain jagged, sensory, and immediate.

Over time this pattern has tightened. The more Matthias avoids darkness, distracts himself, and searches for a reason the accident happened, the more fragile and altered he feels; the more fragile he feels, the more he monitors for danger and braces at ordinary sounds. He finally sought help after startling so badly at a crashing prop case during a daytime production meeting that he knocked over his chair in front of his crew. What frightened him most was not just the embarrassment, but the thought that this was who he is now—someone unrecognizable to himself, always on guard, ruled by images he cannot master. What he hopes, cautiously, is that he can find a way to speak about the accident without being swallowed by it, and return to a set without feeling that catastrophe is about to happen again.
